stem: A 29-year-old woman with a BMI of 37 has daily headaches and brief episodes of blurred vision. Both optic discs are swollen. MRI of the brain is normal, and lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 34 cm H2O with normal fluid. Acetazolamide is started.
oneliner: 29F + BMI 37 + headaches, transient blurred vision + papilledema + normal MRI + opening pressure 34 + acetazolamide started → how does it help?
ask: This drug lowers her intracranial pressure mainly by which of the following?

options.A: Reducing CSF production by the choroid plexus
options.B: Increasing CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
options.D: Shrinking brain water by an osmotic gradient
options.E: Blocking sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle

whyNot.B: No drug opens the granulations; that is a **shunt or venous stent** effect
whyNot.C: Venous pressure falls with **weight loss or venous sinus stenting**

answer: Less CSF made by the choroid plexus
why: **Obese young woman + papilledema + normal MRI + high opening pressure** = idiopathic intracranial hypertension. **Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase** in the choroid plexus, so **less CSF is made**.

drug.name: Acetazolamide
drug.how: Blocks carbonic anhydrase (proximal tubule, choroid plexus, eye)
drug.use: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, glaucoma, altitude sickness, metabolic alkalosis
drug.watch: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias, sulfa allergy

stem: A 66-year-old man with Parkinson disease took levodopa alone and had severe nausea, vomiting and orthostatic dizziness at doses needed to control his tremor. His neurologist changes him to a combination tablet with a second drug that does not cross the blood-brain barrier. His symptoms improve at a lower levodopa dose, with less nausea.
oneliner: 66M + Parkinson disease + levodopa alone gave nausea, vomiting, orthostasis + switched to combination tablet with a drug that stays out of the brain → how does the added drug work?
ask: The added drug improves his tolerance mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.D: Enhancing dopamine reuptake in the striatum
options.E: Inhibiting dopa decarboxylase outside the brain

whyNot.A: **Selegiline**: lengthens dopamine action in the brain; does not cut peripheral dopamine
whyNot.B: **Benztropine**: helps tremor but does not reduce nausea or orthostasis
whyNot.C: **Bromocriptine / pramipexole**: agonists that would not lower levodopa needs this way
whyNot.D: Would **lower** synaptic dopamine and worsen symptoms

why: **Carbidopa does not cross the blood-brain barrier.** It **blocks dopa decarboxylase in the periphery**, so **more levodopa reaches the brain** and less dopamine forms outside it, which cuts nausea and orthostatic hypotension.

drug.name: Carbidopa (with levodopa)
drug.how: Blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, so more levodopa enters the brain
drug.watch: Levodopa effects: nausea, dyskinesias, on-off fluctuations, hallucinations

stem: A 27-year-old woman has a throbbing right-sided headache with nausea, vomiting and light sensitivity that began 2 hours ago. Neurologic examination is normal. She has had similar episodes monthly. She takes a subcutaneous injection that relieves the pain within 30 minutes.
oneliner: 27F + throbbing unilateral headache + nausea, vomiting, photophobia + similar episodes monthly + injection relieves pain within 30 min → how does the drug work?
ask: The injected drug acts mainly at which of the following targets?

whyNot.B: Used for **prophylaxis** (some agents) and psychosis, not for aborting an attack
whyNot.C: **Metoclopramide** helps nausea but is not the main abortive drug
whyNot.D: **Phenylephrine-type** pressor: raises blood pressure, no antimigraine action

why: **Acute migraine with a rapidly acting injection** = **sumatriptan**: a **5-HT1B/1D agonist** that constricts cranial vessels and blocks **CGRP release** from trigeminal nerve endings.

drug.name: Sumatriptan
drug.how: Constricts cranial vessels and inhibits CGRP and other neuropeptide release
drug.watch: Coronary vasospasm (avoid in CAD), chest tightness, tingling; avoid with MAO inhibitors

stem: A 31-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has painful spasms in both legs and stiff legs when she walks. Examination shows increased tone that is worse with fast passive movement, brisk knee reflexes and sustained clonus at both ankles. She is started on an oral drug that acts in the spinal cord to reduce reflex transmission.
oneliner: 31F + MS + painful leg spasms + velocity-dependent tone, brisk reflexes, ankle clonus + oral spinal-cord drug → works how?
ask: The drug most likely works by which of the following mechanisms?

options.C: Inverse agonism at the benzodiazepine site

whyNot.A: **Strychnine** does this and causes violent spasms, not relief
whyNot.C: Inverse agonists cause **anxiety and seizures**; they do not relax muscle
whyNot.D: **Botulinum toxin**: injected into a single muscle, not an oral spinal-cord drug
whyNot.E: Would raise sympathetic tone; **no antispasticity effect**

why: **MS + velocity-dependent tone + hyperreflexia + clonus** = spasticity from an upper motor neuron lesion. **Baclofen** is a **GABA-B (Gi-coupled) agonist** that hyperpolarizes spinal neurons and cuts reflex transmission.

drug.name: Baclofen
drug.how: Activates Gi-coupled GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord; K+ efflux hyperpolarizes neurons and reduces reflex transmission
drug.use: Spasticity from MS or spinal cord injury; intrathecal pump for severe cases
drug.watch: Sedation, weakness; abrupt withdrawal causes rebound spasticity, seizures, fever
